newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Crude port closure exposes Taiwan monopoly's woes.
newsitem.headline: Crude port closure exposes Taiwan monopoly's woes.

text.p: A new closure at Taiwan's only northern crude port and a related slowdown at its only jet fuel refinery are casting harsh new light on festering problems at state monopoly Chinese Petroleum, analysts say.

The utility was forced to close one of two production units at its Taoyuan refinery on Monday due to an unspecified pipeline problem that shut down its tanker off-loading facility, cutting off crude supplies to the refinery.
The offshore port closure forced the 300,000-tonne tanker Vanadis to anchor off northern Taiwan, awaiting repairs that would allow it to unload its cargo of African crude.
The port shutdown comes just three weeks after an August 29 closure at the same facility due to offshore oil leaks.

The incident was Chinese Petroleum's seventh major mishap in 1996, after a string of oil leaks, pipeline ruptures and fires that have cost the oil monopoly more than T$1.1 billion (US$40 million) in compensation claims.
Analysts say the company's problems lie in its operations and monopolistic structure rather than its hardware.
"The monopolised oil market is the real cause of their poor management system and the series of accidents," said economist Ma Kai of Taiwan's independent Chunghua Institute for Economic Research.

A parliamentary committee on Tuesday asked Chairman Chang Tzu-yuan to resign over the accidents and called for Taiwan's top investigative body, the Control Yuan, to investigate the company's operations.
"Chinese Petroleum's real problem is its management," one industry safety researcher said on condition of anonymity.
Analysts say many problems could be solved by privatising the company, a long-term project already under way but not scheduled for completion before 2000.

Chinese Petroleum officials agreed that the closed market provided the oil giant a chance to lose its competitive edge, but also said the central government's direct policy control was to blame for many problems.
"Chinese Petroleum enjoys a monopoly, but we also have to carry out many central government decisions and policies that are not always sound business decisions," a company executive said.
The executive said the selection of the Taoyuan refinery site was a good example of a poor government directive.
"Placing a refinery at northern Taiwan, where strong winter currents often batter the offshore oil unloading and can shut down its operation, was a bad choice," he said.
"It's no wonder we have so many problems with the Taoyuan offshore unloading units," he added.
Because of difficult winter conditions, the refinery is generally forced to run at lowered production levels from September to March, he said.
According to the executive, the central government's decision to build an oil refinery at the north end of the island was intended to balance Taiwan's oil supplies between north and south.
Industry sources said the decision to place one refinery in northern Taiwan also reflected military considerations.
-- Taipei Newsroom (2-5080815)
